paragraphs: The order of washing the hands (netilat yadayim) in the morning: first one takes the vessel of water in the right hand and passes it to the left hand; then one pours water from the vessel that is in the left hand onto the right hand; and after this one holds the vessel in the right hand and pours onto the left hand — that makes one round. One repeats this order a second and a third time, so that each hand is washed three times in total, but one should not wash each hand three times in a row, one after another, since the evil spirit (ruach ra'ah) is uprooted only by washing done in alternation (serugin), as we have written, and as all this is explained in Sha'ar HaKavanot of our teacher the Ari, may his memory be a blessing. Some are meticulous that the right hand should never take the vessel from the left hand at all; rather, after the left hand pours onto the right, it places the vessel on the ground, and the right hand then takes it up from the ground and pours onto the left. But in any case, it is the right hand that gives the vessel to the left each time, so that the left may pour from it upon itself, in order to show the submission of the left before the right, like a master decreeing upon his servant to serve him. And the reason the washing is only on the hands is that the hands and the feet are the extremities and endings of the body, and in a person the five gevurot of Manatzpach spread out, which are the doubled letters, five and five, and corresponding to them are five fingers on the right and five on the left, and this applies to both the hands and the feet; and it is known that the external forces (chitzonim) have no grip except at the endings of the gevurot and the dinim and at their extremities, since they have no power to draw from holiness above except at its ending below — and therefore at night, at the time of sleep, an evil spirit rests upon the hands, for that is where the ending is, and the external forces have the ability to take hold there; therefore one must wash one's hands with water, which is the aspect of chesed comprising five chasadim, and through them the five doubled gevurot of Manatzpach in the fingers of both hands are sweetened, and the kelipot (husks) that had taken hold there are pushed away and depart through the chasadim, for chesed always pushes away the kelipot. And know that were it not for the fingernails placed at the tips of the fingers, the hands would be impure even during the day and even without sleep; but now, because of the fingernails, the evil spirit rests only at night, at the time of sleep, or whenever one enters the bathroom. And if you should ask, if so, why is there no washing for the feet, since the same reasoning applies to them — the Rabbi 'Yafeh Sha'ah,' may his memory be a blessing, answered that the feet are gripped more strongly than the hands, and therefore, because of the strength of their grip, we have no power to push them away by washing; and only the Kohanim, by virtue of the Temple and its service, had the power to push impurity away even from the feet, and therefore it is written of them, “And Aaron and his sons shall wash from it their hands and their feet” (Exodus 30:20). And from this you may understand the reason for the obligation to wash the face, hands, and feet on Erev Shabbat, for the merit of Shabbat has the power to protect. Thus far his words.

clarification.explanation: The order of washing hands in the morning: first one holds the vessel of water in the right hand and transfers it to the left hand; then one pours from the vessel in the left hand onto the right hand; then one holds the vessel in the right hand and pours onto the left hand — this is one complete round. This order should be repeated two more times, so that each hand is washed three times in total — but one should not pour three times in a row on the same hand, since the evil spirit is uprooted only when the washing is done in alternation (switching between the hands), as explained in the writings of the Arizal. Some are meticulous that the right hand should never take the vessel directly from the left hand — rather, the left hand, after pouring onto the right, places the vessel on the ground, and the right hand lifts it up from there. But in any case, it is the right hand that gives the vessel to the left hand before the pouring, in order to show the submission of the left to the right, like a master commanding his servant to serve him. The reason the washing is done only on the hands (not the feet): the hands and feet are the extremities of the body, and the five doubled gevurot (Manatzpach) spread through a person, corresponding to the five fingers on each hand. The impure forces have no grip except at the extremities and endings of gevurah, and therefore at night, during sleep, an evil spirit rests specifically on the hands. Washing with water (the secret of chesed) sweetens the gevurot in the fingers and removes the impure forces. The fingernails at the fingertips protect against impurity resting there even during the day; without them the hands would be impure always. As for the feet — they are not washed because the grip of the impure forces there is stronger, and only the Kohanim, by virtue of the sanctity of the Temple and its service, had the power to push impurity away from the feet as well (hence it is said of them, “And Aaron and his sons shall wash... their hands and their feet”). From this one also understands the reason for washing the face, hands, and feet on Erev Shabbat — by virtue of Shabbat there is additional protective power.
takeaways: Each hand is washed three times in alternation, not three times in a row on the same hand.
The right hand always gives the vessel to the left hand, expressing the left's submission to the right (chesed over din).

Washing is only on the hands, since that is where the impure forces take hold during sleep; the feet are washed only by Kohanim in the Temple service, and, in remembrance of this, also on Erev Shabbat.

paragraphs: One must wash all the fingers and the palm up to the wrist joint. As for the fact that on Yom Kippur and on the Ninth of Av it suffices up to the knuckles of the fingers, Maharai Tzemach, may his memory be a blessing, wrote that on Yom Kippur the evil spirit does not have as much dominion, and on the Ninth of Av it is not particular about such a small amount, since the entire day belongs to it anyway, because of our many sins. Thus far his words.

clarification.explanation: In an ordinary morning washing one must wash all the fingers and the palm up to the wrist joint (not the elbow). But on Yom Kippur and on the Ninth of Av, it suffices to wash only up to the knuckles of the fingers. Maharai Tzemach wrote that the reason is that on Yom Kippur the spirit of impurity does not have as much dominion as on other days, and on the Ninth of Av it is not particular about such a small measure, since that entire day belongs to it anyway (because of our many sins).
takeaways: Ordinary morning washing: up to the wrist. On Yom Kippur and the Ninth of Av: up to the knuckles of the fingers suffices.

paragraphs: After washing three times in alternation as stated, one should rub the hands against each other, as explained in the words of our teacher the Ari, may his memory be a blessing. And although his words are terse, so that it appears a single rubbing suffices, we find that our teacher the Rashash, may his memory be a blessing, required rubbing three times, and arranged kavanot (intentions) for each of the three times; therefore one must be careful to rub three times. And it seems to me that at the time of rubbing one should take care that the fingers be upright, pointing upward, and not bent.

clarification.explanation: After washing three times in alternation, one should rub the hands against each other, as explained in the writings of the Arizal. Although his language suggests that a single rubbing suffices, the Rashash wrote that one should rub three times, and arranged a special intention for each of the three times — therefore one must take care to rub three times. During the rubbing, it is proper to make sure the fingers are upright, pointing upward, and not bent.
takeaways: Rub the hands together three times after washing, not just once.
The fingers should be upright, pointing upward, during the rubbing, not bent.

paragraphs: After the rubbing, do not leave your fingers bent downward; rather, immediately raise your hands and fingers upward and lift them up to the head, or at least lift them up to the level of the face, since the face too is included in the head. And you should recite the blessing “al netilat yadayim” immediately, at the moment you raise and lift your hands, so that the raising of your hands not be in vain, as mentioned in the holy Zohar, that it is forbidden to raise one's hands for nothing (reikanya); and your hands should remain raised and upright until you finish the blessing. This is why the blessing is “al netilat yadayim” (on the lifting of the hands), a term of elevation, as in “and He lifted them and raised them” (Isaiah 63:9), and one does not recite a blessing on “rechitzat yadayim” (washing of the hands). And take care, when you lift your two hands toward the head, to bring the joints of the arms — that is, the elbows, called in the vernacular ‘coudes’ and in Arabic ‘ikas’ — inward, toward the body, in the secret of “and all their backs were toward the house” (I Kings 7:25). One must also spread the two palms of the hands during the blessing, as one who wishes to receive something in them, and this hints at the receiving of purity in them, as our teacher, may his memory be a blessing, wrote in Sha'ar HaKavanot and 'Olat Tamid.'

clarification.explanation: After the rubbing, one must not leave the fingers bent downward; rather, one must immediately raise the hands and fingers upward, at least to the level of the face (which is considered part of the head), and preferably up to the head itself. One should recite the blessing ‘al netilat yadayim’ immediately upon raising the hands, so that the raising of the hands not be in vain — as brought in the holy Zohar, that it is forbidden to raise one's hands without purpose. The hands should remain raised and upright until the blessing is finished. The reason the blessing is ‘netilat yadayim’ (a term of lifting, as in ‘and He lifted them and raised them’) and not ‘rechitzat yadayim’ (washing) is that the main point is the elevation and the lifting. When raising the hands toward the head, one should bring the elbows inward, toward the body (the secret of ‘and all their backs were toward the house’), and one should also spread the palms of the hands during the blessing, like one expecting to receive something — as a hint at receiving purity.
takeaways: Immediately after rubbing, raise the hands and fingers upward, and recite the blessing at once upon raising them.
The hands remain raised until the blessing is finished — hence ‘netilat yadayim’ (lifting), not ‘washing.’
Bring the elbows inward and spread the palms as if expecting to receive something.

paragraphs: According to the opinion of our teacher the Ari, may his memory be a blessing, after washing properly three times in alternation, the evil spirit is completely uprooted; therefore one must recite the blessing immediately, before drying the hands — and not as the Acharonim, may their memory be a blessing, wrote, that it is not uprooted until after drying, and who therefore held that the blessing should be recited after drying. And so it is explicit in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, may his memory be a blessing, to recite the blessing before drying.

clarification.explanation: According to the Arizal, immediately after washing properly three times in alternation, the evil spirit is completely uprooted from the hands, and therefore one should recite the blessing immediately, before drying the hands with a towel. This is unlike the opinion of certain later authorities who wrote that the evil spirit is uprooted only after drying, and who therefore held that the blessing should be recited after drying. The siddur of the Rashash also states explicitly to recite the blessing before drying.
takeaways: According to the Ari and the Rashash: recite the blessing immediately after washing, before drying the hands — since the evil spirit has already been uprooted.

paragraphs: Our teacher, may his memory be a blessing, wrote in 'Olat Tamid,' folio 15b, that when a person wakes from sleep, he must immediately wash his hands before touching his garments at all, and it is also forbidden to walk four cubits without this morning washing, as is written in the Zohar on the verse “to whom God brought it by His hand” (Job 12:6). Therefore every person should take care to prepare the vessels near his bed, so that he not need to walk four cubits. And there are people who, in cold weather, put socks on their feet while still in bed, before rising to perform the washing of the hands, and this is not proper conduct, and they must be warned about this.

clarification.explanation: As soon as a person wakes from sleep, he must wash his hands before touching his garments at all. It is also forbidden to walk four cubits without this morning washing, as explained in the Zohar. Therefore, every person should prepare the washing vessels near his bed, so that he not need to walk four cubits. Some people, in cold weather, are accustomed to put socks on their feet while still in bed, before rising to wash their hands — and this is not proper, and they should be warned about it.
takeaways: One must wash the hands immediately upon waking, before touching clothing and before walking four cubits.
Prepare the washing vessel near the bed in advance.
Do not put on clothing (such as socks) before washing.

paragraphs: If one rises from sleep and does not find a washing vessel near him, but it is placed far away, and he cannot ask another person to bring it to him, he should walk in steps of less than four cubits at a time. And if he rose from his bed and went to the washing vessel near him but did not find in the vessel a sufficient measure to wash three times on each hand — that is, including the palm — and is forced to go far to bring water, he should see whether there is enough of this small amount of water to suffice for washing up to the knuckles of his fingers, like the washing of Yom Kippur; he should wash up to the knuckles of his fingers, and afterward take the vessel and fill it with water and wash properly. And in all this, he should walk in steps of less than four cubits at a time.

clarification.explanation: One who rises from sleep and does not find a washing vessel near him, but only far away, and cannot ask someone else to bring it to him — should proceed in steps of less than four cubits each time. And if he went to the nearby vessel but did not find in it a sufficient amount of water for a full washing (three times on each hand, up to the palm), and is forced to go further to bring water — he should check whether the small amount he has suffices for a partial washing up to the knuckles of the fingers (like the washing of Yom Kippur), and wash accordingly; afterward he should bring a full vessel and wash properly. In every case, he should walk in steps of less than four cubits each time.
takeaways: If no washing vessel is nearby, always walk in steps of less than four cubits at a time.
If there is only a small amount of water, one may first wash up to the knuckles of the fingers and afterward complete a full washing.

paragraphs: Morning hand-washing is not to be done directly onto the ground, but into a vessel, and it is forbidden to pour the washing water in a place where people pass, since an evil spirit rests upon it; therefore one should pour it into a drain of the bathroom or into a drain made in courtyards in the ground, which they call in the vernacular 'bloa.' One must also warn them that sometimes the vessel into which they wash fills up to its brim because of the many members of the household, and then, when they wash into it again, some water is inevitably spilled onto the ground; and if it happens that the washing water is spilled onto the ground, one should pour much clean water onto that ground in order to nullify the washing water that was spilled there.

clarification.explanation: Morning hand-washing must be done into a vessel, not directly onto the ground. It is forbidden to pour the washing water in a place where people pass, since an evil spirit rests upon it — therefore one should pour it into the drain of the bathroom or into a special drain in the courtyard (a drainage pit). One must also be careful, since sometimes, when many members of the household wash from the same vessel, the vessel fills up and overflows, and water inevitably spills onto the ground — and if this happens, one should pour much clean water over that spot in order to nullify the washing water that was spilled there.
takeaways: Washing is done into a vessel, not directly onto the ground.
Washing water should be poured in a designated place (a pit/drain), not in a place where people pass.
If washing water is accidentally spilled on the ground, pour much clean water over that spot.

paragraphs: One should not recite a blessing nor study opposite the washing vessel that contains the washing water, until one removes it or covers it, like the law of urine, since it is more impure than urine.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to recite a blessing or study Torah while a vessel containing the washing water is present opposite oneself, until one removes it from the room or covers it — like the law regarding urine, since the washing water is even more impure than urine.
takeaways: Do not recite a blessing or study Torah while a vessel with washing water stands opposite you — remove it or cover it first.

paragraphs: Every person should take care to instruct his wife to perform hand-washing every day for the small children, even those who are still nursing infants, because sometimes they extend their hands and touch foods and render them impure, so that the sitra achra (the 'other side') rests upon that food; and this custom is also a good segulah for young children, so that they grow up in purity and become 'great ones of holiness,' as mentioned in 'Chesed LaAlafim.'

clarification.explanation: Every person should take care to instruct his wife to perform daily hand-washing even for small children, including nursing infants, because they sometimes extend their hands and touch foods, thereby causing impurity (the sitra achra) to rest upon that food. This custom is also a good segulah for children, so that they grow up in purity and holiness.
takeaways: Accustom even small children, including nursing infants, to daily hand-washing.
This prevents impurity on foods they touch, and is also considered a good segulah for their upbringing in purity and holiness.

paragraphs: One should take care to wash one's face every day, and also rinse one's mouth to remove the saliva that is in it, for besides this being good for the healing of the body, there is in it a mitzvah for the honor of one's Creator.

clarification.explanation: One should take care to wash the face every day, and likewise rinse the mouth to remove the saliva and phlegm that accumulate in it — this is beneficial both for bodily health and is considered a mitzvah for the honor of the Creator.
takeaways: Wash the face and rinse the mouth every day — for health and also for the honor of the Creator.

paragraphs: One should not receive water for washing from one who has not yet washed his own hands, as it is written, “and the pure shall sprinkle upon the impure” (Numbers 19:19); and likewise one should not receive it from a menstruating maidservant, nor from a gentile manservant or maidservant, as mentioned by the Acharonim. And 'Lev Chayim,' siman 65, wrote that one who has washed his hands and afterward touches the hands of another who has not yet washed must go back and wash a second time; and see Kaf HaChayim (Palagi), siman 8, letter 4.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to receive washing water from someone who has not yet washed his own hands, based on the verse ‘and the pure shall sprinkle upon the impure’ (the pure one gives to the impure one, not the reverse). Likewise, one should not receive washing water from a menstruating maidservant, nor from a gentile manservant or maidservant. One who has washed his hands and then touches the hands of another person who has not yet washed must go back and wash again.
takeaways: Do not receive washing water from one who has not yet washed, nor from a menstruating maidservant or a gentile servant.
Touching the hands of one who has not washed nullifies your washing — you must wash again.

paragraphs: If a person sleeps during the day, and likewise if he sleeps after midnight, he requires hand-washing, pouring three times in alternation; but he need not wash into a vessel — he may wash on the ground if he has no vessel before him — and he also need not recite the blessing “al netilat yadayim.” And although Rabbi Maharav Sharabi, may his memory be a blessing, wrote in 'Divrei Shalom' that in this case no hand-washing at all is required, and likewise brought this from 'Mikdash Melekh,' Rabbi 'Emet LeYa'akov,' may his memory be a blessing, already wrote that this was said only in a time of pressing need; rather, the proper and correct practice is that hand-washing three times in alternation is required, but without a blessing. And if he slept his fixed sleep in his bed during the first half of the night, and awoke before midnight, he should perform a complete hand-washing according to the law and recite the blessing “al netilat yadayim.” And if he stayed awake until after midnight, whether at a feast or at work, and did not sleep until after midnight had passed, he too, when he awakens, should perform a complete hand-washing according to its law and recite the blessing “al netilat yadayim.” And although our teacher the Rashash, may his memory be a blessing, wrote in 'Nehar Shalom' that if one sleeps after midnight, the impure spirit does not have dominion over him and no hand-washing is required — he based his words on another consideration he wrote, namely that because one awoke at midnight and drew down the intellects (mochin) through the blessings; and likewise his grandson, Maharav Sharabi, may his memory be a blessing, based this too on the blessings and on engaging in Torah study. Therefore, one who stayed awake until after midnight and did not recite the blessings, and then slept — even according to the opinion of our teacher the Rashash, may his memory be a blessing, requires hand-washing with a blessing. And only if, after midnight, before sleeping, he recited the morning blessings and studied Tikkun Chatzot and engaged in Torah, then when he awakens from his sleep in the morning he should perform hand-washing three times, but should not recite the blessing “al netilat yadayim.” However, if he did not recite the morning blessings and only engaged in Torah study, I am in doubt as to whether he should recite the blessing “al netilat yadayim” or not, and the widespread custom is to recite the blessing.

clarification.explanation: One who sleeps during the day, and likewise one who sleeps after midnight, requires hand-washing three times in alternation, but is not obligated to wash specifically into a vessel — one may wash on the ground if there is no vessel, and one also does not recite the blessing ‘al netilat yadayim.’ There is an opinion (Rabbi Sharabi) that no washing at all is required in this case, but this was said only in a time of pressing need; in practice, it is correct to wash three times without a blessing. If one slept his fixed sleep in bed during the first half of the night and awoke before midnight, he should perform a complete washing with a blessing. Likewise, if he stayed awake until after midnight (at a feast or at work) and slept only after midnight had passed — upon awakening he should perform a complete washing with a blessing. Although the Rashash wrote that one who sleeps after midnight does not need washing at all, since he had awakened at midnight and engaged in the blessings and Torah study (thereby continuing the flow of the mochin) — if someone remained awake until after midnight without reciting the morning blessings and only then fell asleep, then even according to the Rashash's opinion he requires washing with a blessing. Only if, before falling asleep (after midnight), he had recited the morning blessings, studied Tikkun Chatzot, and engaged in Torah study — then when he awakens in the morning he washes three times but without a blessing. In a case where he engaged only in Torah study without reciting the morning blessings, there is doubt as to whether to recite the blessing, and the widespread custom is to recite it.
takeaways: Sleeping during the day or after midnight: wash three times in alternation, not necessarily into a vessel and without a blessing (see the exceptions below).
Sleeping before midnight with waking before it, or staying awake until after midnight and only then sleeping — requires a full washing with a blessing.
One who recited the morning blessings and studied Torah before falling asleep after midnight washes without a blessing; if he did not recite them, the custom is to recite the blessing.

paragraphs: If one did not sleep until after midnight, although according to the opinion of our teacher the Rashash, may his memory be a blessing, he may recite the morning blessings after midnight, nevertheless, since his intention is to sleep after midnight, our custom is not to recite the morning blessings except at a time when we remain awake the entire night, such as the night of Hoshana Rabbah and the night of the festival of Shavuot and the like, when we do recite the morning blessings; and so it is proper to practice, as I have written in my holy book 'Makabtzi'el.'

clarification.explanation: One who has not slept until after midnight — although according to the Rashash's opinion he may recite the morning blessings after midnight as well — our custom is not to recite the morning blessings except at a time when one stays awake the entire night, such as the night of Hoshana Rabbah or the night of Shavuot. This is the proper practice.
takeaways: Custom: the morning blessings after midnight are recited only on nights when one stays awake all night long (such as Hoshana Rabbah, Shavuot).

paragraphs: Before hand-washing, one should not touch with the hands the mouth, the nose, the ears, or the eyes, even if they are closed and one touches them from outside; and if an itch arises in any of the above during sleep, one should scratch through a garment. Also, one should not inhale snuff through the nostrils before hand-washing; and if the craving is very strong, one should get up and wash the hands first, and afterward inhale the snuff. But in daytime sleep, or sleep after midnight, one need not take care of any of the above, even though we have written that one should wash the hands three times.

clarification.explanation: Before the morning hand-washing, one should not touch the mouth, nose, ears, or eyes with the hands (even if closed, from outside). If an itch arises in one of these places during sleep, one should scratch through a garment rather than directly with the hand. One should also not inhale snuff through the nostrils before washing; one who craves it strongly should get up and wash the hands first, and only afterward inhale it. However, in the case of daytime sleep or sleep after midnight, none of these precautions are required (although, as stated, one should still wash the hands three times).
takeaways: Before morning washing: do not touch the mouth, nose, ears, or eyes; scratch only through a garment.
Do not inhale snuff before washing.
These precautions apply only to nighttime sleep, not to daytime sleep or sleep after midnight.

paragraphs: These are the things that require hand-washing three times in alternation because of an evil spirit: one who rises from bed after sleep; and one who leaves the bathroom, even if he did not relieve himself there but entered for some other purpose — however, if he did not enter with his whole body but only extended his hands inside, in order to hand a vessel of water to someone sitting there to wash with, since only a part of him (his hands) entered and not his whole body, an evil spirit does not rest upon him as it does when his whole body enters, but only a small degree of it, and therefore a single washing suffices for him; and one who is stringent to wash even in such a case three times in alternation, a blessing shall come upon him, as I have written in my holy book 'Makabtzi'el.' And likewise one who has marital relations should wash afterward three times, and likewise the woman should wash afterward three times, and likewise one who walks in a cemetery, and one who walks within four cubits of a corpse, and all the more so one who touches the corpse itself, should also wash three times. And as for the practice of the world, that when people wash their hands because of a death, and upon their return from the cemetery, not to dry their hands with a towel but to leave them until they dry by themselves in the air — this is not strictly required by law, but they act so in order not to divert their attention from the remembrance of death; therefore, if it is winter, when there is great and severe cold, and it is very difficult for a person to leave his hand undried by a towel, and he suffers greatly from the cold, he may then dry them with a towel, and there is no harm in it.

And know that even one who enters the bathroom does not have an evil spirit rest upon him with the same intensity as the evil spirit that rests upon him during sleep, which involves 'a taste of death'; therefore one need not be careful in all these matters about not walking four cubits without hand-washing, for one need be careful of this only in the case of sleep. Likewise, one need not be careful in all these matters to wash specifically into a vessel, as I have written regarding hand-washing after sleep; but one must be careful to wash three times in alternation, and also to wash a measure of a revi'it.

clarification.explanation: These are the things that require hand-washing three times in alternation because of an evil spirit: rising from bed after sleep; leaving the bathroom, even if one did not relieve oneself there but entered for another purpose. But if one only extended his hands inside (for example, to hand someone sitting there a vessel of water) without entering with his whole body — since only a part of him (the hands) was there, a lighter form of the evil spirit rests upon him, and a single washing suffices (though one who is stringent to wash three times even here, a blessing will come upon him). Likewise, one who has had marital relations, and likewise a woman — both wash afterward three times. Likewise one who walks in a cemetery, or within four cubits of a corpse, and all the more so one who touches the corpse itself, washes three times. It is customary that when people wash their hands on account of a death (in the cemetery or upon returning from it), they do not dry their hands with a towel but let them dry on their own — this is not strictly required by law, but is done so as not to divert attention from the remembrance of death; however, in winter, when it is very difficult because of the cold, it is permitted to dry with a towel. One should further know that in the bathroom, the spirit of impurity does not rest with the same intensity as in sleep (which involves 'a taste of death'), and therefore there is no need to be careful there about the prohibition of walking four cubits without washing, nor is a vessel specifically required — but one must be careful to wash three times in alternation and with a measure of a revi'it of water.
takeaways: Washing three times in alternation is required after: sleep, leaving the bathroom, marital relations, and walking in a cemetery or near a corpse.
Extending only the hands (not the whole body) into the bathroom requires only a single washing.
In the bathroom, unlike after sleep, there is no requirement of a vessel and no prohibition against walking four cubits — but one must still observe the measure of a revi'it.

paragraphs: And these are the things that require washing because of a slight disturbance (nidnud) of an evil spirit, for which a single washing suffices and three times in alternation are not required: one who leaves the bathhouse, and one who cuts his fingernails, even if he did not cut all of them. And there are those who are stringent that one who cuts his fingernails should wash three times in alternation, in a case where the fingernails protrude beyond the flesh, and their reasoning is plausible according to the kabbalistic secret; and one who is stringent also regarding the bathhouse, to wash three times, a blessing shall come upon him.

And these are the things that require not hand-washing but merely a rinsing of any amount — that is, one washes the hands once, for cleanliness: one who removes or puts on his shoes with hands that touched them, and the same applies if he touches them after putting them on, or after taking them off; however, if he touched shoes that no one has ever worn, even once, there is no concern at all and no washing is required. Likewise, one requires a single washing for cleanliness if he touches his feet or other covered parts of his body; but in exposed parts, such as the face, the back of the neck, and the neck, and likewise the hands up to the end of the forearm, no washing is required. And the left hand, even if one touches the joint adjacent to the arm where the tefillin are placed, up to after two-thirds of that joint, is considered among the exposed parts, and no washing at all is required; but the right hand, on which the hand-tefillin are not placed, if one touches that joint beyond the forearm-joint, requires washing, since it is considered among the covered parts, as it is not customary to handle there; and likewise for a woman, that joint on both her hands is considered among the covered parts, and if she touches it she requires washing. And in a place where women are accustomed to cover the joints of their arms adjacent to the hand — where they customarily place loops near the cuff at the top of their garments so that the garment covers the whole arm — then even if she touches the arm she requires washing for cleanliness. Likewise the breasts, at a time when a mother is nursing her child, since they are customarily always exposed, if she touches them she does not require washing; but if she is not nursing, since they are customarily fully covered, they are then included among the covered parts, and she requires washing if she touches them. Likewise, one who scratches his head or searches his garments for lice, even if he did not find any, and likewise one who touches a louse, requires a single washing for cleanliness.

clarification.explanation: There are things that require hand-washing only because of a slight (nidnud) disturbance of an evil spirit — for which a single washing suffices, not three times in alternation: leaving the bathhouse, and cutting one's fingernails (even if not all of them). Some are stringent to require washing three times in alternation for nail-cutting when the nails protrude beyond the flesh, the reasoning for this stringency being based on the kabbalistic secret; and one who is stringent also regarding leaving the bathhouse, to wash three times, a blessing will come upon him. There are other things that require only a washing for cleanliness (not a formal washing) once: one who takes off or puts on shoes with hands that touched them, whether before or after wearing them — but if he touched shoes that have never been worn, no washing at all is required. Likewise, one who touches his feet or other covered parts of his body requires a single cleanliness-washing, but exposed parts (face, back of the neck, the neck, and the hands up to the end of the forearm) require no washing. The left hand, at the place where tefillin are worn — only up to after two-thirds of that joint (the one near the hand) — is considered exposed and requires no washing; beyond that, in the remaining third (closer to the shoulder), it is considered covered and requires washing. But the right hand (where tefillin are not placed there) is considered covered at that spot, since it is not customarily handled — so touching it there requires washing; and for women, that same joint on both hands is considered covered. In places where women customarily cover the arm-joints near the hand (with loops in the sleeve of the garment), touching there requires a cleanliness-washing. Likewise the breasts, while a mother is nursing her child — since they are customarily always exposed — touching them requires no washing; but if she is not nursing and they are customarily fully covered, touching them requires washing. Likewise, one who scratches his head or searches his garments for lice (even without finding any), and one who touches a louse, requires a single cleanliness-washing.
takeaways: Leaving the bathhouse or cutting fingernails — a single washing suffices (though being stringent to wash three times is praiseworthy).
Touching covered parts of the body (or shoes that have been worn) requires only a single cleanliness-washing; exposed parts require nothing.
The definition of 'covered' vs. 'exposed' depends on actual clothing custom (e.g., the right hand versus the left, or the breasts while nursing).
